<div>
![](https://www.floridamuseum.ufl.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/23/2020/04/Common-Coqui1-web-sized.jpg){.intro_image fig-alt="A common coqui frog on a leaf"}

Long-Term Ecological Research (LTER) datasets are incredibly valuable because they provide a wide variety of ecological data for a system. They are also, unfortunately, often incredibly untidy. Here, we will explore and tidy a modified version of a coqui frog abundance dataset from the [Luquillo LTER](https://luquillo.lter.network/){target="_blank"} in Puerto Rico. Coqui frogs are well known for their mating calls. I highly recommend listening to their calls!

The ten questions draw from every lesson in Module 2. Earlier questions assess individual operations, while later questions combine those operations in complete analyses.

</div>

## About the data

This problem set uses `coqui_counts.rds`, an untidy subset of Luquillo LTER transect data that records coqui frog counts by distance along each transect. You can view the [full dataset and metadata in the EDI Data Portal](https://portal.edirepository.org/nis/mapbrowse?packageid=knb-lter-luq.25.1115151){target="_blank"}.

<button class="accordion">Click this button to learn more!</button>

::: panel

In this problem set, we will explore the file `coqui_counts.rds`. The data are formatted as a tibble data frame with the following variables:

* `site` (character): The study area where an observation occurred;
* `coordinates` (character): The longitudinal and latitudinal coordinates of the site, in decimal degrees, separated by a comma;
* `transect_id` (numeric, integer): A numeric identifier for the transects that were sampled;
* `habitat_class` (character): A code for the type of habitat where a transect occurred (e.g., G = "gap", G-E = "gap edge", F = "forest", E = "forest edge");
* `habitat` (character): The type of habitat where the transect occurred;
* `date` (date): The date of a given sampling event;
* `count_0-10m` (numeric, double): The number of coqui frogs observed in the first 10 meters of the transect;
* `count_10-20m` (numeric, double): The number of coqui frogs observed in the second 10 meters of the transect;
* `count_20-30m` (numeric, double): The number of coqui frogs observed in the third 10 meters of the transect;

:::

## Subsetting and extraction

::: now_you
2\. The same column can be subset as a one-column data frame or extracted as the vector stored inside it. Please:

* Pipe `coqui` into a function that subsets the data frame to the `coordinates` column, then pipe that result into `class()`.
* Pipe `coqui` into a function that extracts the `coordinates` column, then pipe that result into `class()`.
* In a comment, describe how the two operations and their resulting classes differ.

Do not assign either result to a name.

*Hint: You will find the tools for this question in **2.1 Introduction to subsetting and extraction**.*
:::

## Data tidying and mutation

Remember, data exploration should almost always occur in the console pane. Keep only your answers in your script file.

::: now_you
3\. The columns `coordinates` and `habitat_class` are each a problem of a different kind. A location has separate longitudinal and latitudinal variables, while `habitat_class` redundantly encodes the same attribute as `habitat`. In a single piped statement:

* Split `coordinates` into `longitude` and `latitude`.
* Convert both new columns to the numeric class in a single function call.
* Remove `habitat_class` from the data frame.
* Globally assign the result to the name `coqui_no_class`, then remove the name `coqui` from your global environment.

*Note: Changing the class of a column is a data cleaning step rather than a tidying step (see **2.6 Tidy data**).*

*Hint: You will find the tools for this question in **2.4 Reshaping data frames**, **2.6 Tidy data**, and **2.1 Introduction to subsetting and extraction**.*
:::

::: now_you
4\. Each count observation was made on a given date, at a given distance along a given transect. The three count columns spread the variable `distance_class` across column names and place three count observations in each row. In a single piped statement:

* Pivot the count columns into the variables `distance_class` and `count`. Remove the redundant `count_` prefix from the values of `distance_class` as part of the pivot.
* Add the logical column `detected`, which indicates whether `count` is greater than zero.
* Globally assign the result to `coqui_long`, then remove the name `coqui_no_class` from your global environment.

*Hint: You will find the tools for this question in **2.4 Reshaping data frames** and **2.2 Introduction to mutation**.*
:::

## Grouped operations and summarizing

::: now_you
5\. In a single piped statement:

* Choose a grouping method and group `coqui_long` by `site` and `distance_class`. In a comment, explain why that grouping method is appropriate for the operations below.
* Add `mean_count`, the mean count within each group, while retaining every row.
* While the grouping remains, subset to count observations that exceed their group mean.
* Remove the grouping, then subset the result to `site`, `transect_id`, `date`, `distance_class`, `count`, and `mean_count`.

Do not assign the result to a name.

*Hint: You will find the tools for this question in **2.3 Grouped operations and summarizing**.*
:::

::: now_you
6\. In a single piped statement:

* Choose a grouping method and return the proportion of count observations in which at least one coqui frog was detected and the number of count observations within each combination of `habitat` and `distance_class`. Name the summary columns `detection_rate` and `observations_per_distance`. In a comment, explain why that grouping method is appropriate for this analysis.
* Pivot the summary wider so that the values of `distance_class` form column names and `detection_rate` supplies their values. Retain `observations_per_distance` as a column.

Do not assign the result to a name.

*Hint: The mean of a logical vector is the proportion of its values that are `TRUE`.*

*Hint: You will find the tools for this question in **2.3 Grouped operations and summarizing** and **2.4 Reshaping data frames**.*
:::

## Data visualization

As always, we should visualize our data early and often.

::: now_you
7\. Plot the count observations through time:

* Pipe `coqui_long` into `ggplot()`. Map `date` to the x-axis, `count` to the y-axis, `habitat` to color, and `distance_class` to shape.
* Add a point geometry.
* Set the four habitat colors and three distance-class shapes manually. Choose colors that remain distinguishable for a reader with a color vision deficiency.
* Label the x-axis `Date`, the y-axis `Coqui count`, and the plot `Coqui counts through time`. Give both legends informative titles.
* Create one facet for each site.
* Apply `theme_bw()`.

*Hint: You will find the tools for this question in **2.5 Introduction to data visualization with ggplot2**.*
:::

## Ranked subsetting

::: now_you
8\. Return the observation with the largest count within each combination of site and distance class:

* Use a ranked subsetting function with a per-operation grouping argument. If the largest values are tied, return only one of the tied rows.
* Subset the result to `site`, `distance_class`, `transect_id`, `date`, and `count`.

Do not assign the result to a name.

*Hint: You will find the tools for this question in **2.1 Introduction to subsetting and extraction** and **2.3 Grouped operations and summarizing**.*
:::

## Tidy data and relational tables

::: now_you
9\. Explore the observational levels in `coqui_long`:

* Return the distinct combinations of `site`, `longitude`, and `latitude`.
* Return the distinct combinations of `transect_id`, `site`, and `habitat`.
* In a comment, name the tidy data rule that `coqui_long` violates. Identify the variables that uniquely identify a site, a transect, and a count observation, and explain how the two code blocks support your conclusion.

*Hint: You will find the tools for this question in **2.1 Introduction to subsetting and extraction** and **2.6 Tidy data**.*
:::

::: now_you
10\. Repair the violation that you identified above:

* Create a table with one row per site and globally assign it to the name `sites`.
* Create a table with one row per transect and globally assign it to the name `transects`.
* Create a table containing only the variables required to describe and identify each count observation, and globally assign it to the name `counts`. The derived variable `detected` does not need to be stored.
* Before running the final code, write a comment that predicts its number of rows. Then write one piped statement that joins `counts`, `transects`, and `sites` in that order. Confirm in a second comment whether the result agrees with your prediction.

*Note: A join that returns more rows than expected matched at least one key more than once (see **2.4 Reshaping data frames**).*

*Hint: You will find the tools for this question in **2.6 Tidy data**, **2.1 Introduction to subsetting and extraction**, and **2.4 Reshaping data frames**.*
:::
